item.description: I didn’t know my last baby was my last baby. We had talked about our last baby, sure, but not in certain terms. item.title: I’m Not Just Raising a Child—I’m Raising a Bridge
item.description: Some days feel heavier than others. You watch them grow and wonder if the world sees all of them—the heart, the heritage, the story stitched into their very bones, or only pieces that fit its narrow boxes. You hear the questions before they even do: “Where are you really from?” “Why do you look like that?” and your chest tightens because you know the answer is both simple and infinitely complex. item.description: A few weeks ago, I made a mistake no mother of a teenage driver wants to make: I watched from the window as my son drove away without his cell phone. item.title: Children Are a Work In Progress—So Are Their Mothers
item.description: For a long time, I assumed a mom always knew exactly what to say to her children in every possible situation. She could guide her children through life’s roughest waters, bearing the weight of their pain and anguish without so much as a flinch. I wasn’t sure how moms learned to do this; maybe it was instinct, or perhaps some secret course they took before having babies? But when I was a little girl, rocking my baby dolls to sleep, I prayed I’d somehow figure it out so I could be a good mom too.
